A signal with net alpha t of 2.2 standalone can still add materially as an orthogonal component or as an execution-scheduling overlay (avoid trading into transient retail-driven pressure), and the plan as written would not measure that.
issues.what_breaks: The evaluation stage terminates on a standalone test, so a genuine effect that fails the standalone hurdle produces no usable output despite the data to assess its marginal contribution already being in hand.
issues.fix: Add one step: regress the RLOIB strategy's net returns on the in-house existing signal ensemble to report marginal information ratio, and report the signal's ability to predict same-name transient price pressure at the horizons the execution desk trades over, as a separate deliverable from the standalone alpha.

result.overall: This is a well-matched plan for this firm — right horizon, right acceptance criteria (cost, capacity, breakeven cost as a headline rather than an asserted Sharpe), a genuine pre-committed falsifier that separates 'lot filter adds nothing' from 'real but unharvestable', and it correctly treats the round-lot-equals-retail premise as something to test rather than inherit. The gaps are refinements, not repairs: the cheapest possible kill (does the round-lot residual have any independent variation, and is round-lot share stationary across 2015–present) should be a day-one gate with a numeric threshold rather than buried in the identification stage; there is no mechanism-derived negative control on retail intensity, so a generic reversal effect could be reported as a retail one; and entry timing plus crowding — the two things that actually decide harvestability for this book — are left implicit. Fix those four and it is worth the quarter.

result.plan_implied_asker: a microstructure research group at a large systematic equities firm with full TAQ, proprietary exchange feeds and a replication platform
result.what_would_falsify: Pre-committed and explicit: lift <2.0x (or bootstrap LB <1.5x) on Rule 605 accounting / Hui-Walter; recall <35%; signing accuracy <70% (hard stop <60%) vs RLP-flagged known-side prints; mean stock-day r <0.40 vs sub-penny label or <0.25 vs VandaTrack; |t|<3 on round-lot imbalance incremental to Benchmark-A imbalance in the forward-return panel. Author also states H0 as his own prior (round lots are an institutional scheduler signature) and commits to publishing the negative result plus a map of better identifiers.

issues.summary: Five hard gates joined by AND, with thresholds asserted rather than derived from what the signal would need, will kill a usable identifier in a setting where the missed-effect error is the expensive one.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This is a diversified systematic book judged on whether a signal survives costs across ~2,000 names; a false positive dies in the replication platform, a false negative is a permanently forgone sleeve. Yet the design requires G1 AND G2 AND G3 AND G4 AND G5 to pass in a single venue partition, then applies Benjamini-Hochberg on top. Nothing in the plan connects recall ≥35% to tradability: a round-lot filter with 15% recall and 5x lift across 2,000 names produces plenty of signal-days, and 15% recall on an unbiased subsample of retail is a perfectly good instrument. The same is true of the 70% signing floor — 65% signing with 4x lift is economically live.
issues.what_breaks: The Phase 1 → Phase 2 decision. Under conjunctive gating the joint pass probability is far below any individual gate's, so the most likely outcome is a kill that reflects threshold calibration rather than the absence of retail content, and Phase 2 never runs.
issues.fix: Derive the thresholds from economics rather than convention: state, for a given lift/recall/signing triple, the implied information ratio of a round-lot imbalance signal on this universe, and gate on that composite rather than on each component. Replace the AND with a scored decision (e.g. proceed if the implied signal-to-noise clears a stated bar in any partition), and drop BH correction on gates that are already pre-registered and directional — it double-counts conservatism.

issues.summary: G4's r ≥ 0.40 threshold is set against a benchmark whose error rate the plan itself documents, with no attenuation correction, so a perfect identifier could fail it.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan states Benchmark A has sign-error rates 'in the tens of percent' and is degraded by midpoint migration — and then requires mean stock-day correlation ≥0.40 against exactly that label. With 20–30% sign errors plus low recall, observed correlation is attenuated well below true agreement; the plan invokes latent-class estimation precisely for this reason at G1 but not at G4. The VandaTrack gate at 0.25 is worse: it is a daily, sample-based, name-limited aggregate correlated against stock-day series.
issues.what_breaks: G4 becomes a coin-flip gate that, under the conjunctive structure of the previous issue, can single-handedly kill the project for measurement reasons rather than economic ones.
issues.fix: Express G4 as noise-corrected agreement (attenuation-corrected r using the label error rates estimated in G1, or a latent-class kappa) and state the threshold in those units. Also front-load the feasibility check the plan flags but does not schedule — confirm the RLP flag exists in historical, not just live, feeds before G3/G4 are designed around it, since both anchors collapse if it does not.

issues.summary: The one test that establishes whether the identification question has any economic stakes (does round-lot imbalance add anything beyond standard order-flow imbalance and existing retail proxies) sits last, behind four label-quality gates.
issues.why_it_applies_here: On this firm's infrastructure the G5 panel — forward returns on Benchmark-A imbalance plus round-lot imbalance with double-clustered SEs — is a couple of days of work on data already licensed, far cheaper than assembling RLP flags across seven venues and running Hui-Walter. The plan's stated reason for deferring it (avoiding a retrofitted retail story) is legitimate but does not require the test to be last, only that its thresholds be pre-registered, which they already are.
issues.what_breaks: Weeks of exchange-feed acquisition and label triangulation are spent before knowing whether round-lot imbalance carries any incremental predictive content at all. If it does not, the identification result is a publication, not a trade, and the project should have ended in week one.
issues.fix: Run G5 in parallel with Benchmark C in the first week, with a pre-registered kill: if round-lot imbalance is not incrementally predictive of forward returns net of a standard OFI control, stop — the retail-attribution question is academic for this book. Keep the identification gates as the interpretive layer, not as a prerequisite.

issues.summary: Identification is validated entirely in the pre-half-penny, fixed-100 regime, but any resulting signal would trade under the tiered round-lot definition and the new tick regime.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The sample is deliberately 36 months ending before half-penny compliance because Benchmark A only survives there. But the plan's own H0 turns on retail routing behaviour (dollar/fractional orders arriving as odd lots) and on where the round-lot boundary sits — both of which the amendments change directly. A 100-share threshold that is diagnostic when 100 is the universal round lot means something different when the round lot is 40 or 10 shares at high prices.
issues.what_breaks: Phase 2 signal construction. Gates could pass on a definition of 'round lot' that no longer exists at deployment, and the retail/institutional separation could invert if schedulers re-slice to the new tiers.
issues.fix: Add a post-compliance out-of-time check using Benchmark B alone (RLP flags survive the regime change; sub-penny does not) on a shorter recent window, as a required condition before Phase 2. Report lift/recall/signing under both the fixed-100 and tiered definitions in the recent window, not just the historical one.

issues.summary: G3 measures signing accuracy on RLP-flagged lit executions, a subpopulation that is unrepresentative of where the bulk of retail flow actually prints.
issues.why_it_applies_here: RLP flow is the slice retail brokers route to exchanges rather than sell to wholesalers — a selected residual, and the plan itself says its recall is 'very low'. Most retail volume in this sample period is internalized and prints to the TRF. Signing accuracy estimated on RMO-certified lit prints need not transfer to TRF round lots, yet G3 is one of the two hard stops.
issues.what_breaks: G3 either passes or fails for reasons specific to a small, selected venue population, and that verdict is then applied to the off-exchange partition where the signal would actually live.
issues.fix: Estimate signing accuracy separately within each partition, using the Rule 605 buy/sell composition and latent-class machinery for the TRF partition rather than importing the RLP-derived number; make the hard stop partition-specific and state explicitly which partition the Phase 2 signal would be built in.

issues.summary: Phase 2's go/no-go criteria specify after-cost Sharpe, worst year and net/gross but never state a return horizon, a capacity figure or a crowding check — the three things this firm actually judges signals on.
issues.why_it_applies_here: 'Forward returns' in G5 and 'directional continuation' in Phase 2 are left unspecified, and the sign of the trade depends on it: at intraday horizons the economics are liquidity provision against uninformed flow, at weekly horizons the published retail-imbalance effect runs with retail, not against it. The firm's horizon is days to weeks, so the plan must commit to which claim it is testing. Separately, retail concentration is not uniform across the universe, so capacity is the binding question for a flow-inference signal, and the plan's own pitfall about retail drifting toward systematic day-trading is exactly a crowding argument it never tests.
issues.what_breaks: A Phase 2 pass at Sharpe 1.0 with unspecified horizon and no capacity estimate is not a result this committee can act on; net/gross >0.40 constrains cost but says nothing about size.
issues.fix: Pre-specify the horizon grid (e.g. 30min / 1d / 5d / 20d) and state which horizon the mechanism predicts and with what sign. Add a capacity condition to the go/no-go (turnover-scaled notional at which net/gross degrades below 0.40) and a crowding check — correlation of the round-lot imbalance signal with published retail-imbalance and short-term-reversal factors.

result.overall: This is a well-built plan and unusually honest: it separates identification from profitability, states the author's own prior as the null, front-loads a spreadsheet-only test that can kill the project in a week, pre-commits falsifiers, and pairs the one sophisticated method with arithmetic the committee can check. The real risk is not credulity but the opposite — five conjunctive hard gates with thresholds that were asserted rather than derived, one of them uncorrected for label noise the plan itself documents, in a setting where a missed real effect is the expensive error; the most likely outcome as written is a false kill. Recalibrate the gates against implied signal economics, move the incremental-return test to week one alongside Benchmark C, and add a post-compliance RLP-only check so the result transfers to the regime it would trade in.

result.plan_implied_asker: A larger fundamental shop with a multi-analyst deep-dive team and prior-cycle history at hand, able to spend a quarter reconstructing four industry episodes
result.what_would_falsify: Stated negative criteria: negative implied gross bookings two consecutive quarters; channel inventory >1.5x normal; a backlog/LTA definition change in a quarter that would otherwise have declined; supplier finished-goods inventory rising two quarters while backlog is called record. Plus the explicit prior that announcement count alone carries no information.

issues.summary: The decisive, cheap checks are buried inside a large simultaneous pipeline with no stated order or early gate.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Three checks resolve most of this question in days: does the company disclose RPO at all and under what ASC 606 policy; has any customer cash arrived (contract liabilities, deposits, reservation fees, capex funding on the cash flow statement); and what durable horizon is already embedded in EV via reverse DCF. If there is no cash and no minimums, the whole tiering/coverage/backtest apparatus is moot. The plan lists these alongside peer and prior-cycle reconstruction as if equal cost.
issues.what_breaks: One analyst at a five-person shop starts with the RPO roll-forward and prior-cycle calibration and spends weeks before learning whether the commitments are cash-backed — the single fact that determines the answer.
issues.fix: Restate as a gated sequence: Week 1 = RPO policy footnote + customer cash trace + reverse DCF implied horizon. Pre-commit that if no customer cash and no binding minimums appear, the work stops and the answer is 'announcements, not durability.' Everything else is conditional on passing that gate.

issues.summary: The 'LTA-to-RPO gap' is treated as the key signal without first establishing what this company's RPO policy actually excludes.
issues.why_it_applies_here: ASC 606 practical expedients let issuers exclude contracts under one year and variable consideration allocated to wholly unsatisfied performance obligations, and some issuers exclude cancellable amounts entirely. Shortage-era LTAs are frequently indexed-price or cancellable-with-notice, i.e. precisely the population an issuer would exclude. The gap between announced LTA value and RPO would then be a disclosure-policy artifact, not evidence of weak claim strength — and could equally be large for a genuinely strong book. The plan inherits the interpretation from the question without testing it.
issues.what_breaks: The tiering step ('in RPO' is an attribute in five of six tier definitions) and the coverage math both mis-rank claim strength; a strong contract book reads as Tier 3, or a weak one reads as Tier 1 if the issuer happens to include cancellable amounts.
issues.fix: Read the revenue recognition footnote's stated RPO exclusions and practical-expedient elections first, and note any change in that policy across the sample. If the exclusions swallow the LTAs, drop 'RPO inclusion' as a scoring attribute and rely on contract language plus received cash.

issues.summary: Haircut percentages presented to two significant figures but calibrated from realized conversion data that is not externally observable.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Companies do not publish backlog-to-revenue conversion rates or cancellation experience; the 2021–23 semiconductor episode gives at most inferred, company-specific fragments. Yet 90–95%/70%/25–35% multiply directly into coverage, which is then compared to hard gates of ≥60% NTM and ≥40% year-two. A ±15-point uncertainty in the Tier 2 haircut flips the gate.
issues.what_breaks: The threshold test at the end of the plan looks quantitative but its verdict is set by an unverifiable parameter, and the IC cannot inspect the calibration because the underlying data does not exist.
issues.fix: Present coverage as a band across a low/base/high haircut grid and require the constructive/negative conclusion to be invariant across the band. State explicitly where each haircut came from, and where it is judgement rather than calibration.

issues.summary: Net bookings solved as a plug, then cancellations 'backed into' from the same identity — underdetermined, and it drives one of the four kill criteria.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The roll-forward has one equation and several unobservables: FX, M&A, contract modifications, reallocation between the 12-month and remainder buckets, and policy-driven exclusions all land in the same residual. Unless the company separately discloses bookings or book-to-bill, 'negative implied gross bookings' can be produced by a modification or an FX swing rather than hidden cancellations — and it is a pre-committed negative criterion, so a spurious firing kills a position.
issues.what_breaks: The negative-criteria gate rejects on an artifact; conversely a real cancellation wave is masked by an offsetting M&A addition.
issues.fix: Only use this criterion where bookings or book-to-bill is independently disclosed. Otherwise reduce it to a flag that triggers a transcript/footnote hunt for the explanation, not an automatic negative.

issues.summary: RPO trajectory cannot be reconstructed for two of the four backtest episodes, and the backtest as scoped is a quarter of analyst time.
issues.why_it_applies_here: ASC 606 RPO disclosure begins in 2018–19; telecom 2000 and memory/passives 2017–18 have no RPO to trace, only company-defined Item 101 backlog with no comparability. The plan's stated backtest output — 'RPO trajectory, realized vs implied coverage' — is unobtainable there. Meanwhile reconstructing four episodes plus peers plus customer mirror tables is not a one-analyst task at a shop with two analysts covering 25–30 names.
issues.what_breaks: Either the analyst burns weeks and returns a backlog-only comparison mislabelled as coverage evidence, or the backtest is quietly abandoned and the haircuts lose the only calibration they claimed.
issues.fix: Cut the backtest to 2021–22 semiconductors plus the live AI-cycle names where RPO exists, and reframe the pre-2018 episodes as qualitative base rates on backlog conversion and pricing rolloff only. Cap the whole exercise at a stated number of analyst-days.

issues.summary: Two mandatory constructive conditions may be structurally unobservable, so the gate can auto-fail a genuinely good situation.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Customers' purchase-obligation tables are aggregate and do not name suppliers, so 'mirror disclosures reconciling to ≥50%' is only measurable when a customer separately names this company in a release or 8-K — often not the case. Segment-level coverage requires RPO or LTA value allocated by product line, which issuers rarely disclose, forcing analyst allocation into a threshold test. Requiring all six conditions makes any single unobservable condition a rejection.
issues.what_breaks: The threshold step returns 'not constructive' for reasons of disclosure availability rather than business quality — a false negative dressed as discipline — or the analyst fills the gap with an allocation assumption and the gate becomes self-fulfilling.
issues.fix: Split the six conditions into must-haves that are always observable (cash support, contract language on minimums and take-or-pay, top-3 concentration, implied-vs-modeled horizon) and corroborators used when available (mirror reconciliation, segment split). State that missing corroborators widen the required margin on the must-haves rather than triggering rejection.

result.overall: The economics here are unusually well thought through for this asset class: it separates announced commitment from enforceable commitment, insists on customer cash as the real test, prices the residue against market-implied durability, and pre-commits four falsifiers plus a correct warning that duration without growth is a downgrade. The problems are ordering and scale, not thinking — the two facts that decide the question (what the company's RPO actually excludes, and whether any customer cash has arrived) sit inside a pipeline that also asks one analyst to rebuild four industry cycles, two of which predate the disclosure the method depends on, and the hard coverage gates are driven by haircuts no external data can calibrate to the precision quoted. Reorder into a one-week gate — RPO policy footnote, contract-liability/deposit trace, reverse DCF implied horizon — run the full register and tiering only if cash and minimums are actually there, and show coverage as a band rather than a point against a 60% line.

result.plan_implied_asker: A multi-analyst macro/commodity research shop with standing subscriptions to industrial price series, customs data and a dedicated cross-cycle historian
result.what_would_falsify: Episodes where contracted price stayed materially above spot for 8+ quarters after supply normalization in the absence of a hard qualification moat — that would break the "honored in volume, broken in price, split by switching cost" thesis. Plus pre-registered HBM checks (contract-liability direction, RPO growth threshold, customs shipments, customer obligation tables) resolvable within 12 months.

issues.summary: The plan builds a cross-industry framework and never applies it to the company that prompted the question.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The question is whether THIS name's shortage guidance implies durable revenue. Every data item listed — supplier 10-Ks, customer obligation tables, price series — is scoped to the 20-30 analog episodes. No step establishes the subject's requalification lag, whether its parts are single-sourced mid-program or fungible, what its RPO and contract-liability lines currently say, what its customers' purchase-obligation tables show, or how its LTA book behaved in its own prior cycle. The plan's own thesis says the switching cost, not the label, is the variable — so the subject's placement on that axis is the whole answer, and it is the one thing not measured.
issues.what_breaks: Step 4-6 produce base rates and a capacity ledger for other markets; the output ('probability-weighted haircut') then has to be assigned to the name by assertion. If the subject sits at the aerospace-forging end, the entire fragility thesis is irrelevant to it; if at the container end, most of the episode work was unnecessary.
issues.fix: Add as step 0, before any episode work: determine the subject's qualification lag and alternate-source availability from customer engineering disclosures and its own filings; pull its RPO/contract-liability and top customers' purchase-obligation tables for this cycle and the prior one; document how its last cycle's commitments resolved. If the subject has a prior comparable shortage, that record outranks any cross-industry base rate and should be the primary evidence.

issues.summary: Scale and data spend are not executable by one analyst at a five-person shop and are committed before any cheap test.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Twenty-five to thirty episodes coded on ten contract features across three outcome dates, plus Exhibit 10 contract reading, plus PACER/Chancery/ICC/SIAC/foreign court dockets, plus per-market capacity ledgers with ramp curves and hidden capacity, requires TrendForce, Fastmarkets, Benchmark, UxC, Argus/ICIS, Drewry/Xeneta, Panjiva or ImportGenius and the SEMI fab database. That is a six-figure data bill and multiple analyst-quarters at a shop with two analysts, no engineers, and nobody who maintains a database. Neither the capacity ledger nor the customs reconciliation is maintainable in Excel over a 3-5 year hold.
issues.what_breaks: The work either stalls partway with an incomplete episode set — at which point the base rates are whatever subset got finished, i.e. worse than no base rate — or consumes the analyst for a quarter on a position decision that has to be made now.
issues.fix: Cheap version, one analyst, 2-3 weeks, no new licences: (a) the subject-specific work in issue 1; (b) three analog episodes chosen for closest qualification profile to the subject, not the widest spread — read the actual contract exhibits and trace price and volume for eight quarters past the peak using Bloomberg series already on the terminal; (c) one page on what the current multiple embeds about duration. Commission the wider episode study only if (b) shows the subject's category is genuinely ambiguous.

issues.summary: Both validation tests are circular: the holdout outcome is already known and cited in the plan, and the negative-control test re-derives the criterion the cases were selected on.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan proposes holding out the 2021-2024 auto-semi cycle and predicting outcomes 'before checking' — while itself already citing the ~$16bn LTSA figure, the Renesas-Wolfspeed deposit, and 'the 2023-2025 correction.' The outcome is in the analyst's head. Separately, aerospace forgings are labelled 'best case: hold' and MLCC/containers 'worst case' in the episode list, and then the stated validation is 'test that aerospace/LNG score durable and MLCC/containers fragile.' A framework built to explain outcome-labelled cases will reproduce those labels by construction.
issues.what_breaks: The validation step produces a pass regardless of whether the switching-cost mechanism has any predictive content, and the IC will be shown a framework certified by a test it could not fail.
issues.fix: Drop the auto-semi holdout and rely on the live HBM pre-registration, which is genuinely out-of-sample — but recognise it resolves after the decision. For the historical work, replace validation-by-reproduction with a blind step: have the second analyst score qualification lag and sourcing for each episode from pre-normalization filings only, with outcome data withheld, then compare rankings to realised outcomes.

issues.summary: Conditional base rates rest on an outcome-bracketed, cycle-clustered sample; the probability weights will not survive scrutiny.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The episode list was assembled by naming known cases to span a range ('best case', 'worst case', 'upper bound'), so unconditional frequencies from it are not base rates. And the episodes are not independent draws: containers 2021-23, ABF 2021-23, auto semis 2021-24, lithium 2022-24 and HBM 2023-26 are largely one post-COVID demand shock; MLCC 2017-19, DRAM/NAND 2017-19 and lithium 2017-20 are largely another. Effective N is three or four shocks, not thirty. Conditioning on qualification lag × sourcing × credit × pricing then leaves cells of one or two. The plan's own pitfall list names demand-driven-shortage vs supply-shock-in-flat-demand as 'likely the dominant variance driver' but no design step separates them.
issues.what_breaks: Step 4 and the 'probability-weighted haircut' output attach numerical probabilities to cells with n≈2 drawn from a sample chosen to bracket outcomes. An IC that spots this discards the whole exercise.
issues.fix: Keep the ranking, drop the probabilities. Present as an ordered set of named case comparisons with the subject placed between the two nearest analogs, and state the sample was chosen for range rather than representativeness. Cluster episodes by macro shock and report whether the switching-cost ordering holds within each shock separately.

issues.summary: The step that could resolve the question in days sits behind a multi-quarter pipeline, and nothing is actionable before the position decision.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The thesis is explicitly bimodal on one variable — in-term requalification feasibility. For a single name that is a days-long determination from teardown reports, customer qualification disclosures and one or two industry calls. Placing it nowhere while episode coding, capacity ledgers and breach arithmetic run first means the analyst learns the answer's category last, and the HBM pre-registration checks resolve in twelve months against guidance that lands next quarter.
issues.what_breaks: By the time steps 5-6 finish, the guidance has been either confirmed or broken by reported results and the multiple has re-rated either way.
issues.fix: Sequence: subject qualification lag → subject and customer contract disclosures → nearest three analogs → only then broader base rates and capacity ledger, and only if the subject is genuinely ambiguous. Commit up front to what the analyst tells the IC in three weeks.

result.overall: The analytical core is unusually good: a real variant view stated against what the market is paying for, a genuine falsifier, negative controls derived from the mechanism, ranked rather than regressed inference, and a haircut rather than a fabricated P&L — all of which suits a sceptical IC. But it is written for a research shop three times this size, and it never actually analyses the company that prompted the question: the one determination that decides the answer, whether the subject's product can be requalified in-term, appears nowhere. Send it back scoped to the subject plus three closest analogs, using data already on the terminal, and drop the probability weights and the self-confirming validation.

result.plan_implied_asker: A concentrated fundamental long-only shop doing filings-and-Excel work on one holding, where being wrong about the cost base is the risk that matters
result.what_would_falsify: Reconciled spend plus the inverted sensitivity showing that the uplift required to breach the guided margin floor or miss consensus by 2% is far above any plausible vendor increase — i.e. total impact under ~25bps — at which point tone is declared uninformative and the hypothesis is dropped (with a separately logged, non-thesis open question).

issues.summary: The comparable-customer uplift distribution that produces the 'central case' — the number that triggers the call — cannot actually be observed, so percentile precision is manufactured.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Enterprise licence renewal uplifts for named customers are essentially never disclosed by either party. Step 3 proposes a median/75th/90th percentile from 5–10 comparables built out of vendor NRR, RPO-vs-billings and analyst-firm commentary. NRR blends seat expansion, cross-sell and price across the whole book; RPO versus billings does not cleanly separate price from volume for one contract. The plan then feeds this fabricated distribution into a decision rule ('central case over ~75bps forces a call') and pre-states 15–30% in the hypothesis before any work, so the anchor is set before evidence.
issues.what_breaks: Step 3 and the comparison in Step 5 ('compare to Step 3's distribution'). The whole call ends up resting on a judgment dressed as an estimated percentile, and the IC cannot distinguish the two. The 75th-percentile-as-median adjustment compounds an invented number rather than correcting it.
issues.fix: Drop the percentile framing entirely. Keep only the inversion: solve for the uplift required to breach the guided floor / miss consensus by 2%, then ask a small number of checkable questions — what has the vendor's published list price done over three years, what did this company's own last two renewals do to the line, what does an ex-procurement or SAM consultant say the vendor is asking of similar accounts. Present the uplift as a bounded judgment with named sources, not a distribution.

issues.summary: Step 2 — self-declared the highest-priority input — names sources that will not contain the information: a vendor licence is not filed as a material contract by the customer.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan correctly identifies metric changes (per-server to per-core, bundling, audit settlement) as where the step-function tail lives, and says that is the highest priority. But it proposes to find price-protection caps, true-up rights, MFN and audit clauses in material-contract exhibits and prior 8-Ks. Ordinary-course vendor agreements are not material to a $400M-cap-relevant customer and are not filed; risk factors will be generic. The one party who knows is management, and management is the reason for the question.
issues.what_breaks: Step 2 returns nothing on the specific negotiated terms, so the metric-change scenario in Step 5 gets populated with assumptions and then quoted in bps as though modelled. The tail case — the only branch that is thesis-relevant for a 3–5 year holder — becomes the least evidenced part of the output.
issues.fix: Name the sources that do exist: the vendor's published licensing rulebook and price list (these are public for the major enterprise vendors and define what metric shifts are even possible), one expert-network call with an ex-procurement/SAM person on that vendor's current playbook, and a direct IR question on the licensing metric basis and whether price protection survives the new term. If none of these resolve it, say so and carry the metric-change tail as an unquantified position-risk question rather than a bps figure.

issues.summary: The cheapest test of whether public data can answer the question at all — can the last renewal be seen in the reported expense lines — sits in Step 4 and in validation, behind the sizing and mechanics work.
issues.why_it_applies_here: On the plan's own hypothesis the licence is mid-single-digit percent of opex and a 15–30% uplift phases over years. That is very likely below the visible noise in a reported opex line. If the prior renewal produced no detectable inflection over four quarters, the back-test proposed under Validation ('predicts the realized move within error bars') cannot be run — and that finding also tells you the current renewal will not be observable ex post either, which changes what the work can deliver.
issues.what_breaks: The single named validation step may be unexecutable, discovered only after Steps 1–3 are sunk. The plan would then have a sensitivity table with no external calibration and no stated fallback.
issues.fix: Run the detectability check immediately after top-down sizing: pull the last two renewal dates and look at the relevant expense line for four quarters after each. If nothing is visible, stop calling it a back-test, state that ex-post confirmation is unavailable, and shift the standard to internal consistency (top-down/bottom-up reconciliation plus the inversion) declared up front.

issues.summary: Scope is disproportionate to the stated base case, and the expensive stages are not gated on the branch that would justify them.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan itself concludes the base case is 30–90bps — 'material to a quarter, not the thesis' — for a manager holding three to five years. Against that, GSA/Crown Commercial schedule triangulation, LinkedIn headcount reconstruction, RFP postings, migration NPV with integration-points costing, and covenant headroom are several analyst-weeks out of a two-analyst shop. Covenant headroom in particular only matters if the impact is an order of magnitude above the hypothesised range.
issues.what_breaks: Analyst time is the binding constraint here, not compute. The plan spends it uniformly across branches rather than concentrating it where the answer changes the position.
issues.fix: Make the branch explicit: Days 1–3 are purchase obligations plus segment opex to bound spend, single-source yes/no, and the inversion for required uplift. Only if the required uplift falls inside plausible vendor behaviour, or the vendor is single-source with a live metric-change route, do Steps 3–5 in full. Drop covenant headroom and migration NPV from the base path.

issues.summary: For a three-to-five-year holder the decision-relevant quantity is the repricing path across successive renewals, not one renewal's quarterly bps.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan is framed around near-term margin and consensus EPS impact, which is the right answer to the question as asked. But the reason this matters to a five-year position is whether vendor share of opex ratchets each cycle because switching cost has grown — which is exactly what Step 4's reconstruction of two or three prior renewals would reveal if extended forward rather than used only for calibration.
issues.what_breaks: The output can be truthfully 'immaterial this year' while the structural trend is the real finding, and nothing in Step 5 surfaces that.
issues.fix: Add one row to the Step 4 output: licence spend as a percent of opex at each of the last three renewals, and the implied path at the next two if the observed ratchet continues. That is a two-hour addition and is the number the IC should actually see.

issues.summary: The 'is it a sign of weakening fundamentals' half of the question is discharged by an immateriality finding plus a logged open question, when a cheap discriminating check exists.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The argument that tone in a live negotiation is uninformative is correct and well made. But it is a claim about tone on this topic; it does not test whether the defensiveness was topic-specific. If disclosure granularity on this vendor line degraded relative to prior years' same-topic answers, or if management was evasive across several unrelated topics on the same call, those point in opposite directions and neither is a negotiation artefact.
issues.what_breaks: If Step 1 shows immateriality, the plan concludes 'tone moot' and files the discomfort, which is exactly the pitfall it lists but does not resolve.
issues.fix: Add a one-hour transcript comparison: prior three years' answers on this same vendor/licence topic, and other topics on the same call, scored on granularity of what was actually disclosed rather than on tone. Pre-commit that degraded specificity on this topic only supports the negotiation explanation; degraded specificity across topics escalates independently of the bps answer.

result.overall: This is a well-built plan for this firm: it refuses the tone trap and replaces it with a materiality question, it front-loads the sizing test that can kill the idea in days, it pre-commits thresholds (25bps / 75bps) and an inversion that an IC can inspect in Excel, and its pitfalls list shows genuine engagement with being wrong. The two things to fix before starting are input feasibility: the comparable-customer uplift 'distribution' cannot be observed and would anchor the call on a manufactured number, and the contract mechanics it calls highest-priority are not in the customer's filings — they have to come from the vendor's published licensing rules and one ex-procurement call, or be carried as unquantified. Cut the base path to sizing plus single-source plus inversion (about three days), gate the rest on that, and add the successive-renewal ratchet, which is what actually matters to a five-year position.

result.plan_implied_asker: A systematic quant shop with an NLP research stack building a reusable cross-sectional text signal
result.what_would_falsify: Stated and genuine: H1 true / H2 false (elevated vendor-topic evasiveness with no predictive content for GM surprise), plus failure of the known-outcome falsification set (~40 bad vs ~40 benign renegotiations), placebo topics, and the post-conclusion-call test for the NDA explanation. The falsifier is defined for the panel signal, not for the single-name call the IC has to make.

issues.summary: The question is about one company's near-term margin risk; the plan's centre of gravity is a 40,000 firm-quarter generalizable text signal.
issues.why_it_applies_here: H2, the panel regression, the decile-sorted sector/size-neutral portfolio, the elastic-net weights and the 2005-2016/2017-present out-of-sample split exist to establish that evasiveness predicts GM surprises broadly. None of that is required to answer whether this issuer's licence renewal threatens gross margin more than management said. The case-specific work that would actually answer it — purchase-obligations tables, Item 1A redlines, the vendor's own filings and pricing, >10% customer disclosure — is listed once and never sequenced or given a decision rule.
issues.what_breaks: Every stage after transcript tagging serves the wrong deliverable. The IC gets a signal-validation report, not a margin exposure estimate, and gets it months after the renegotiation resolves.
issues.fix: Recast as a single-name exposure study: quantify the licence's share of COGS, bound the price increase from the vendor's disclosed pricing and the issuer's purchase-obligations trend, translate to gross-margin bps, and compare to what consensus GM already embeds. Read the trailing eight calls by hand for vendor commentary as one supporting input, not as the study.

issues.summary: Nothing in the plan can be built or maintained by this firm, and the resulting score cannot be inspected by the IC.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Two PMs, two analysts, one ops person on Bloomberg and Excel, no engineers, nobody maintaining a database. The plan requires 500 plus 1,000 hand-labels with kappa targets, a pinned embedding model, a temperature-0 LLM run in triplicate with majority voting, spaCy parse filtering, elastic-net logistic fitting, block bootstrapping at 2,000 draws, two-way clustered plus Driscoll-Kraay SEs, and Romano-Wolf stepdown — plus two transcript vendors and Visible Alpha, CRSP, Compustat and IBES licences. The output the IC would be asked to act on is a standardised composite of five feature families, which is precisely a model it cannot inspect.
issues.what_breaks: The project either never gets built or gets half-built by one analyst for a quarter, and the composite score is rejected at committee on the first question about how deflection was labelled.
issues.fix: Kill the pipeline. If linguistic evidence is wanted, do it manually: one analyst reads the vendor Q&A exchanges from the last eight calls plus this one, tabulates side by side which questions got a number and which got a redirect, and puts the transcript excerpts in the IC memo. That is inspectable and takes two days.

issues.summary: The plan never states what consensus or the sell side currently assumes about this renegotiation, so it cannot say where the view diverges.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The framing question is explicitly whether the risk is worse than management has communicated — a variant-view question. Visible Alpha GM consensus appears only as a regression outcome, never as the benchmark for what is already priced. Defensiveness on a live contract negotiation is visible to every analyst on the call; if brokers have already cut GM for a step-up, elevated evasiveness confirms consensus rather than diverging from it.
issues.what_breaks: Even a clean H1 result produces no actionable conclusion, because there is no statement of what the market believes to contrast it against.
issues.fix: Start by pulling the Visible Alpha GM path and the last three broker notes' treatment of vendor cost, and write down the implied assumed price increase. The deliverable is the gap between that and the bounded exposure estimate.

issues.summary: Evasiveness score is treated as the measure of margin risk without validating the proxy on this name, where the direct exposure is disclosable.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The target is a gross-margin outcome driven by a contract price. That is partly observable: purchase-obligations tables, the vendor's published price changes, capitalised software and the licence's COGS share. The plan substitutes a linguistic score whose link to this issuer's margin is established only through a pooled panel average, and the ≥1.5 SD H1 test is scaled by that firm's own call-to-call variation — a within-firm baseline built from calls in which no renegotiation was underway.
issues.what_breaks: The within-firm and within-call baselines cannot separate 'evasive because it is going badly' from 'evasive because a live negotiation is under NDA' in a sample of one. The post-conclusion-call test resolves it only after the outcome is public, i.e. after the decision is needed.
issues.fix: Anchor on the direct exposure first and use language as corroboration only. If the bounded worst-case price increase cannot move gross margin by a material amount, the tone question is moot and the work stops there.

issues.summary: The measurement gate may make the target name untestable, and this is checked last rather than first.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan requires ≥3 vendor exchanges and ≥150 words per call, ≥4 prior calls per speaker, and a trailing-eight-call vendor-topic baseline, else it reports 'insufficient evidence'. For a single issuer whose vendor licence only became a call topic because it is being renegotiated now, trailing calls plausibly contain zero or one vendor exchange, and the CFO may have changed inside the window.
issues.what_breaks: Months of pipeline construction can terminate in 'insufficient evidence' for the one name that matters, with nothing delivered.
issues.fix: Hour one: open the last eight transcripts and count vendor/procurement exchanges and speaker continuity. If the baseline does not exist, abandon the measurement framing immediately and go straight to disclosure-based exposure work.

issues.summary: Statistical thresholds are calibrated to a pooled panel the decision does not rest on, while the N=1 decision has no stated judgement rule.
issues.why_it_applies_here: |t|≥2.5 out-of-sample, ≥15bp effect, ≥5pp base-rate lift and Romano-Wolf correction are demanded of a 40,000 firm-quarter panel, while the actual IC question — is this issuer's margin at more risk than communicated — gets no pre-committed pattern that would count as confirming or refuting. The panel N is manufactured by pooling issuers whose vendor relationships are not comparable, purely to have something significance-testable.
issues.what_breaks: The plan can pass all its statistical gates and still leave the PM without a defensible position on the name; or fail them and leave the single-name risk unassessed.
issues.fix: Replace the significance apparatus with a judgeable single-name standard: an explicit bps range for the licence step-up, the consensus-embedded assumption, and a pre-stated threshold above which the position is trimmed.

issues.summary: Flow-through timing of the licence repricing is never modelled.
issues.why_it_applies_here: A renegotiated licence hits reported gross margin on the contract's effective date, possibly with step-ups, prepaid amortisation or capitalisation, not evenly across t+1 to t+4 as the outcome definition assumes. For a three-to-five-year holder, whether this is a one-year step-down or a permanent structural cost shift is the decision-relevant distinction, and the plan measures neither.
issues.what_breaks: Even a correct directional read gets mapped to the wrong quarters and the wrong severity, and the panel outcome window may straddle the effect.
issues.fix: Establish the contract term, renewal date and accounting treatment from the 10-K and prior disclosure, then state whether the hit is transitory or structural before any measurement of tone.

result.overall: The question is a single-name, near-term margin risk call for a five-person Bloomberg-and-Excel shop, and the plan answers a different question — does executive evasiveness predict gross-margin surprises across a 40,000 firm-quarter panel — using machinery (LLM-anchored labelling, elastic net, block bootstrap, Driscoll-Kraay, Romano-Wolf, decile portfolios) that this firm cannot build, cannot maintain, and cannot defend to its own committee. The design is internally thoughtful and its falsifier and placebo structure are genuinely good, which makes it a strong plan for a quant firm and the wrong plan for this one; it also never says what consensus assumes about the renegotiation, so it has no route to a variant view. The cheap version, executable by one analyst in a week: count and read every vendor/procurement exchange in the last eight transcripts by hand, pull the purchase-obligations table trend and Item 1A supplier redlines, take the vendor's own disclosed pricing and margin commentary, bound the licence step-up in gross-margin bps, and compare that to the Visible Alpha GM path — if the bounded worst case is immaterial or already embedded, the idea is dead and the tone question never needs answering.

result.plan_implied_asker: A multi-manager alt-data pod trading quarterly SaaS prints, with a data engineer, a licensed web-panel stack, and a systematic risk framework
result.what_would_falsify: Stated and genuine: (a) the MAU model fails to beat benchmark C (two-way FE without MAU) out-of-sample on Diebold-Mariano and on rolling-origin/leave-one-company-out; (b) refitting on excluded consumption-priced names gives equal performance. Also a pre-committed retreat if beta collapses under company trends.

issues.summary: The firm cannot execute or defend this: it requires a maintained 900-1,000 company-quarter panel, three web-panel vendors, and CIPS/Westerlund/Bai-Perron/wild-bootstrap/Diebold-Mariano machinery, in a shop with two analysts, Excel, and no database.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Specific to this plan: it names point-in-time-stamped MAU snapshots from Similarweb plus Datos/Verto/Sensor Tower, wildcard-subdomain hostname rollups, tiered LHS splicing on overlap ratios, and six inference variants. Each of those is a build-and-maintain task, not a one-off pull. The IC's gate is stated as a DM p-value on clustered absolute-error differentials — a statistic nobody in the room can reproduce or challenge, so it cannot carry a decision no matter what it returns.
issues.what_breaks: Data assembly and Estimation. Either the work never finishes, or one analyst produces a black box whose headline number the IC has to accept on faith; the first hostile question ('what happens to Adobe if you drop it?') cannot be answered without a rebuild.
issues.fix: Kill the panel. Cheap version, one analyst, two weeks: take the 3-6 seat-based SaaS names actually held or on the candidate list, buy a single-vendor trial of app-level monthly uniques for their authenticated hostnames back 20 quarters, and put one page per name showing MAU YoY against reported subscription-revenue YoY. Judge it on sign agreement, count of correctly called inflections, and lead length, by eye. If two of the panels are visibly broken by re-basings or desktop-client leakage, that answers the question for a few thousand dollars.

issues.summary: Horizon is wrong twice over: h ∈ {0,1,2} quarters is a print-forecasting window for a three-to-five-year holder, and it is shorter than the ratable-recognition lag between seat additions and reported subscription revenue.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's own vocabulary gives it away — 'never trade within two quarters of a break', 'expect edge in smaller-cap names, decaying', 'split performance by year before scaling capital'. That is a next-print exercise. Separately, for tiers 2 and 3 the LHS is annualized subscription revenue, which is recognized ratably off annual contracts; a seat added in month 1 shows up as roughly a trailing-twelve-month average of seats. The relationship MAU has with that series is dominated by lags of 3-6 quarters, not 0-2, and disclosed ARR (tier 1) is a point-in-time snapshot with completely different timing. Fitting all three tiers on the same 0-2 horizon window mixes two different timing structures.
issues.what_breaks: Estimation and the whole validation block. Beta at h ∈ {0,1,2} on a ratably-recognized LHS will look attenuated or spuriously contemporaneous, and the 'best horizon' choice becomes an artifact of which LHS tier each name happens to sit in. Worse, even a clean win at one quarter tells this firm nothing it can hold for four years.
issues.fix: Reframe the deliverable to what this book needs: does a sustained break in portal MAU trend precede a break in ARR growth trajectory by 2-6 quarters, within name? Test h out to 6, separately by LHS tier, and drop all trading/decay/capital-scaling language.

issues.summary: The load-bearing premise — that panel MAU on the tracked hostname measures the billed seat — is never validated against any company disclosure, and for a large fraction of the named universe the billed seat does not transit a browser at all.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The universe as listed includes Adobe (desktop apps), Zoom and RingCentral (native clients/softphones), Workday and Salesforce (heavy mobile and native), Figma (desktop app). For these the app.* hostname sees a minority of licensed activity, and the share seen drifts as vendors push native clients — exactly the 'MAU-per-seat drifting slowly' assumption the hypothesis says the mechanism requires. Enterprise SSO under-panelling is listed as a pitfall to control for, but it is not a control, it is the question. Meanwhile several names in the list disclose seats, paying customers, or usage metrics directly, and the plan never checks the panel against them.
issues.what_breaks: Data assembly, upstream of everything. Every subsequent test — cointegration, ECM, DM — is applied to a series that may be measuring browser-versus-native mix rather than seats, and no amount of inference machinery detects that.
issues.fix: Make this step one and make it a kill gate: for the handful of names with disclosed seat/paying-customer/DAU series, plot panel MAU against the disclosure and compute the correlation of YoY changes. If the panel does not track disclosed units where units are disclosed, the study is over in a week. Only names passing that check enter the sample.

issues.summary: The plan pre-specifies a menu of fallback specifications with instructions on which to trade if the primary collapses, which guarantees a survivor in a setting where a false positive cannot be diversified.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Named in the plan: three horizons plus a joint lag chosen on out-of-sample fit; levels, YoY differences, and ECM, with 'trading only the differenced or ECM result if beta collapses' under company trends; regime splits or positive-surprise-only restriction if the shelfware interaction is asymmetric; pre-break history dropped or spliced. That is a large search over ~40 effective clusters with an explicit rule to fall back rather than stop. For a 25-30 position book taking three-to-five-year concentrated risk, the cost of adopting a mined specification is a wrong business call held for years — the errors are not symmetric here, and the apparent statistical rigor is masking the real exposure.
issues.what_breaks: Estimation into Validation. The rolling-origin gate cannot repair specification search conducted upstream of it, and 'report all three horizons' is not the same as pre-committing to one.
issues.fix: Pre-commit, in writing before the data is touched, to one horizon, one functional form, and one LHS tier as the primary test, with everything else reported as robustness only and no promotion path. State explicitly that collapse of the primary under company-specific trends kills the thesis rather than routing to the ECM.

issues.summary: The consumption-name negative control would fire against a true hypothesis, because logins plausibly predict revenue for usage-metered vendors more strongly than for seat-metered ones.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Snowflake, Datadog, MongoDB, Confluent bill on volume that is generated by the same users logging in; a positive MAU-revenue relationship there is expected under any theory, so 'equal performance sinks the thesis' sets up a falsifier that is likely to kill a real seat effect. Credit the instinct to build a negative control, but this specific one is derived from the wrong part of the mechanism.
issues.what_breaks: The Falsification step. A correct thesis gets discarded, or the result gets rationalized after the fact — which is worse, because the falsifier was pre-announced.
issues.fix: Pick controls where the stated mechanism genuinely cannot operate: admin-console-only portals (usage decoupled from billed units), per-endpoint or per-device pricing (CrowdStrike), and known shelfware-heavy deployments where seats are provisioned and unused. Predict the sign and magnitude difference in advance rather than testing for 'equal performance'.

issues.summary: For multi-product vendors the tracked portal covers a minority of the revenue on the left-hand side, and the LHS tiering mixes three different constructs across the panel.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Adobe, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Workday and Twilio each report subscription revenue spanning many products; app.* MAU for one portal is being regressed on a total that the portal never touched, and the covered share changes as product mix shifts. Meanwhile tier 1 (disclosed ARR), tier 2 (annualized subscription revenue) and tier 3 (total less professional services and license) are three different quantities with different volatility and different timing, pooled into one beta.
issues.what_breaks: Data and Estimation. The pooled beta becomes an average across names where the numerator explains 80% of the denominator and names where it explains 15%, and the 0.4-0.8 prior on beta has no interpretation across that mix.
issues.fix: Restrict to single-product-dominant, single-portal names where the tracked app plausibly covers the majority of subscription revenue, and to one LHS tier. Report the covered-revenue share per name explicitly as a table the IC can read.

issues.summary: Multi-vendor panel and Visible Alpha licensing is committed before any evidence that the series is usable, at a spend level that is material for a $400M shop.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan calls for Similarweb plus Datos or Verto plus Sensor Tower/data.ai plus Visible Alpha line-item history across 35-60 names and 20+ quarters, with point-in-time snapshots. That is a six-figure annual commitment for a five-person firm, and none of it is contingent on the hostname-coverage or re-basing checks, which sit in the Pitfalls section at the end.
issues.what_breaks: The budget, before the first informative output exists. If Bai-Perron-style step changes turn out to be pervasive across the named universe — which vendor re-basings routinely make them — the spend is sunk against an unusable series.
issues.fix: Single-vendor trial on 5 names first. Inspect the raw monthly series by eye for step changes and for coverage of the authenticated hostname. Only license breadth after that passes.

issues.summary: Beating published sell-side consensus is treated as establishing edge, but the marginal informed buyer of these names already licenses the same web panels.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's incrementality test is the MAU model's error versus cross-analyst dispersion from Visible Alpha. Analysts largely do not run these panels; the funds trading the print do, and quarterly SaaS nowcasting off Similarweb/Datos is among the most widely purchased alt-data uses in the market. So a win against analyst dispersion is compatible with zero information versus price. The plan never asks who is on the other side.
issues.what_breaks: The Validation claim of an edge, and the 'expect edge in smaller-cap names, decaying' assertion, which is an unsupported economic claim the design produces nothing to justify.
issues.fix: For a three-to-five-year holder the honest framing is not near-print edge at all: it is whether portal usage improves the firm's judgement about multi-year seat expansion durability that consensus models linearly. Test that framing, drop the decay and capital-scaling language, and if a near-print claim is retained, check post-print drift rather than error versus analyst estimates.

result.overall: The econometrics are competent but the plan was written for a different firm: a pod shop with a data engineer, a licensed panel stack, and a one-quarter trading horizon. This firm has none of that and holds names for three to five years, so even a clean result at h=1 answers a question they do not trade, and the DM-test gate is not something the IC can inspect or defend. Two substantive defects would also bite at any firm: the premise that panel MAU on app.* measures the billed seat is never validated against the seat disclosures that exist and is implausible for the desktop/native-client names in the list, and the horizon window is shorter than the ratable-recognition lag on the revenue-derived dependent variables. Kill the panel and run the cheap version — 3-6 relevant names, one vendor, one chart per name of MAU YoY against subscription-revenue YoY, judged on inflection calls and lead length — which either establishes the relationship or kills it in two weeks for a fraction of the proposed spend.

result.plan_implied_asker: A systematic alt-data hedge fund with data engineers, trading quarterly earnings prints
result.what_would_falsify: Pre-committed gate: seat-growth-on-MAU-growth beta must be positive, nonzero at 5% under company-block bootstrap, inside [0.5,1.5], pooled within-company partial correlation >=0.45 and positive in two-thirds of firms, stable across halves and leave-one-out; plus coverage-ratio drift >10%/yr kills level work and residual SD >0.15 drops a company. Gate failure is pre-committed to yield a negative result and a taxonomy of why, explicitly not a MAU-versus-revenue fallback.

issues.summary: The execution stack — multi-vendor point-in-time panel vintages, fixed-effects ridge with nested CV, empirical-Bayes shrinkage, Driscoll–Kraay/Clark–West inference — cannot be built, staffed or maintained by this firm, and the IC cannot inspect the object that carries the decision.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Five people, no engineers, no database owner, Bloomberg and Excel. The plan requires ingesting and version-controlling monthly vintages from Similarweb/Comscore/M Science/Yipit plus Sensor Tower/data.ai, maintaining a device-graph deflator per company, an event log of domain and product changes, and an expanding walk-forward with a four-quarter tuning embargo. That is a two-person data engineering function, standing, not a project. And the final estimate the IC is asked to trust is a ridge coefficient shrunk toward a pooled prior — untraceable to any single company by construction.
issues.what_breaks: Every stage after data assembly. In practice the vintage discipline lapses within two quarters, the walk-forward silently becomes an in-sample fit on restated panel data, and the IC declines the output because it cannot be reconstructed by hand.
issues.fix: Strip to what one analyst can hold in a spreadsheet: 6-8 disclosers, one panel vendor, monthly authenticated-path MAU against the disclosed seat metric, per company, plotted. Per-name YoY correlations and coverage-ratio trends as the deliverable. No ridge, no shrinkage, no Diebold–Mariano. If a pooled elasticity is wanted, a single OLS with company dummies and clustered errors is defensible to an IC; the penalized/shrunk version is not.

issues.summary: The deliverable is a quarter-end nowcast benchmarked against pre-print consensus, which is not a horizon this firm trades and is the single most crowded use of web-panel data.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Positions are held three to five years across 25-30 names. A Delta-4-ln(ARR) estimate published five business days after quarter end, scored on RMSE versus damped persistence and on surprise-space sign hits, is a print-trading product. It also puts the firm into direct competition with the buy-side clients who already license exactly these panels for exactly this purpose — the crowding question is never raised, and 'beat pre-print consensus' is the one edge claim that is least likely to be available to a $400M long-only paying retail rates for a Similarweb seat.
issues.what_breaks: The entire validation section. Even a clean pass produces a metric — RMSE reduction versus persistence on a one-quarter growth rate — that no PM here can act on, while the question they actually need answered (does portal activity lead multi-year seat expansion and net retention inflections) is never tested.
issues.fix: Re-specify the target as the multi-year object: does MAU growth lead disclosed seat growth by 2-4 quarters, and does a sustained MAU deceleration precede multi-quarter seat/NRR deterioration? Score it as hit rate on turning points across the 8 disclosers over 20+ quarters, per name. Drop consensus surprise, DM/Clark–West and the five-day nowcast entirely.

issues.summary: The gate pools seat constructs that are not the same object — ADP pays-per-control, Paycom clients x employees, Dropbox paying users, Atlassian seat-tier mix — and derives its statistical power from that pooling.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Pays-per-control is a payroll billing count driven by client employment; Dropbox paying users are individual and SMB subscriptions; Atlassian seat tiers are banded and step-priced. The portal population differs even more: ADP and Paycom portals are logged into overwhelmingly by employees who are not billable seats in any direct sense, while Dropbox logins are approximately the billable unit. A single beta across these is an average of three different mappings, and the 5% bootstrap test, the [0.5,1.5] band and the two-thirds-of-firms rule all get their N from stacking them.
issues.what_breaks: The gate. It can pass on the strength of two or three well-mapped names while the elasticity is meaningless for the rest, and the empirical-Bayes step then actively pulls the badly-mapped companies toward that misleading pooled prior.
issues.fix: Judge each company on its own record over time — sign, rough magnitude and stability of the MAU-to-seat relationship name by name — and report the count of names where it holds rather than a pooled coefficient. Only pool within a genuinely common construct (e.g. self-serve paid-user businesses) and say so.

issues.summary: The value of the work lies in applying the mapping to companies that do not disclose seats, but the mapping is estimated only where seats are disclosed, and the transfer assumption is never tested.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The gate sample is defined as 'seat-like disclosers'. Companies disclose a seat or user count when it is clean, definable and growing, and stop when it is not — Dropbox's paying users and Atlassian's tier mix exist precisely because they are tidy. The plan's only treatment is keeping past disclosers' full windows and testing beta in the last four quarters of a disclosure regime, which addresses when disclosure stops, not whether disclosers' portal-to-seat geometry resembles non-disclosers' at all.
issues.what_breaks: The step where the calibrated beta is carried to a portfolio name that does not disclose seats. In a concentrated book with three-to-five-year holds, that is where a false positive turns into being wrong about the business, and nothing in the design would catch it.
issues.fix: Pre-commit that the output applies only to names with a disclosed seat-like series to validate against, or add an explicit transfer test: for the ex-disclosers, does the beta estimated in the disclosure window still reconcile with subsequent revenue after disclosure stopped? If it does not, say the method does not travel and stop there.

issues.summary: No placebo distinguishes 'authenticated MAU measures billable seats' from 'web traffic co-moves with any company growth metric'.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The design's own logic implies the effect should be specific to post-login paid surfaces and to seat-linked revenue. Consumption-metered and end-customer-portal companies are excluded from the sample rather than used as discriminating cases, and pre-login marketing traffic — the obvious placebo — is only used as a paid-surface split, never as a competing predictor. Company fixed effects and a common time effect do not absorb firm-level growth momentum, which drives both traffic and seats.
issues.what_breaks: Interpretation of a passing gate. A beta near 1 with a 0.5 partial correlation is fully consistent with panel traffic being a generic growth thermometer, in which case it adds nothing over revenue trend and will fail exactly when the company inflects.
issues.fix: Run two cheap controls in the same spreadsheet: (a) pre-login/marketing-page traffic growth as the regressor instead of authenticated MAU — if it performs comparably, the seat story is not what is driving the result; (b) the same regression on 2-3 consumption-priced names, where the seat mechanism cannot apply, as a check that the relationship is not universal.

issues.summary: Multiple panel licences and historical point-in-time vintages are committed at the front, before the cheap coverage check that could kill the idea has been run — and retrospective vintages are usually not sold at this firm's scale.
issues.why_it_applies_here: 'Vintages day one' plus a primary and a replication panel plus two mobile vendors is a five- or low-six-figure annual data spend for a $400M shop, and archived as-was monthly panel vintages are typically an enterprise/systematic product, not something available with a standard Similarweb or Sensor Tower subscription. The plan's own strongest kill test — coverage ratio (panel MAU / disclosed seats) trended per company, with >10%/yr drift killing level work — needs one vendor, eight tickers and current-as-reported history, not vintages.
issues.what_breaks: The walk-forward validation, if vintages turn out to be unpurchasable: it then silently runs on restated panel data and overstates out-of-sample performance. And the spend is sunk before enterprise blindness (Atlassian desktop clients, SSO, VPN-hosted consoles) has been shown to be survivable.
issues.fix: Week one: confirm vintage availability and price in writing, and run the coverage-ratio trend on a single-vendor trial for the 8 disclosers. Only then commit to a second panel or mobile data. If vintages are unavailable, drop the out-of-sample-forecast framing and present the work as a within-name descriptive lead-lag study, stated as such.

result.overall: The statistical design is careful — pre-committed thresholds, a real falsifier, a variance decomposition published before model results, and a coverage-ratio kill test placed early — but it has been written for a systematic fund with data engineers trading quarterly prints, not for a five-person long-only holding names for three to five years. Two things sink it as written: the deliverable is a five-day post-quarter nowcast scored against consensus, which this firm cannot act on and cannot win, and the pooled elasticity stacks incomparable seat constructs (pays-per-control, Dropbox paying users, Atlassian tier mix) to manufacture the N its significance tests rely on, then would carry that average to non-disclosing names where the mapping was never estimated. The version worth doing costs one analyst three weeks and one panel subscription: for the 6-8 disclosers, plot authenticated portal MAU against the disclosed seat series name by name, check whether the coverage ratio is stable and whether MAU turning points lead seat turning points, and check that pre-login traffic does not do the same job — if the ratio drifts or the placebo works equally well, kill it and say so.

result.plan_implied_asker: A mid-sized systematic equity quant shop with data engineering, NLP staff, and factor-portfolio infrastructure
result.what_would_falsify: Stated explicitly and well: the null that peer-relative tone adds nothing beyond SUE, the (-1,+1) announcement return, momentum and style factors; a single-touch 2023-24 holdout against a dated pre-registered primary specification; Harvey-Liu-Zhu t>3.0 with deflated Sharpe; and break-even cost under 30bp declared a paper result. It also names the real failure mode (week-eight t-stat hunting) and accepts a clean null as an output.

issues.summary: The plan cannot be executed by this firm at all — it assumes a data engineering and NLP team that does not exist here.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The firm is five people: two PMs, two analysts, one ops, on Bloomberg/Excel/filings, with nobody who maintains a database. The plan requires Xpressfeed/Snowflake ingestion, domain-adaptive masked-LM pretraining on 1.5-2B transcript tokens, a two-annotator-plus-adjudicator labelling program with Krippendorff alpha, 150k LLM silver labels, TAQ time-weighted spreads, Markit borrow files, CRSP/Compustat/I-B-E-S point-in-time merges, and a pre-written evaluation harness under version control. Not one of those steps is inside this firm's operating envelope, and none of it can be outsourced piecemeal without someone here maintaining it quarter after quarter.
issues.what_breaks: Every step from Data onward. The project either never starts, or a vendor builds a black box the firm pays for and cannot update, revalidate, or debug when coverage changes.
issues.fix: Rewrite as an analyst-executable study: Bloomberg/company-website transcripts for the ~30 holdings plus 5-10 named peers each, Loughran-McDonald or a purchased off-the-shelf tone field in Excel, and a manual Q&A-versus-prepared split. If the answer genuinely requires a fine-tuned transformer on Russell 3000, the honest recommendation is to buy a vendor signal on trial and evaluate it, not to build one.

issues.summary: A 1-3 month signal with documented decay by month 6 is irrelevant to a book held three to five years.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The primary horizon is three months with decay measured at 1/2/6/12, overlapping monthly Jegadeesh-Titman cohorts, and entry at t+1 close. This firm holds 25-30 names for three to five years and turns over a handful of positions a year. Even a true, t>3 effect at that horizon is fully dissipated inside the first few percent of their holding period, and their turnover budget cannot harvest it.
issues.what_breaks: The Portfolio section produces a quintile long-short with monthly rebalancing — an object this firm can neither trade nor short (long-only, no borrow relationship, and the plan's own short leg needs Markit borrow data).
issues.fix: Reframe the dependent variable to something the horizon can use: does a large negative habitual-tone deviation in Q&A precede a 12-24 month deterioration in fundamentals (revenue/margin/guidance revisions) or a multi-quarter peer-relative de-rating? That is a different and, for this firm, more valuable test — and it changes the data requirements substantially.

issues.summary: The headline input is a fine-tuned DeBERTa score the investment committee cannot inspect, and the plan's inspectable outputs are model diagnostics rather than business reasoning.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The IC is explicitly skeptical of models it cannot inspect, and what kills this firm is being wrong about a business. The plan's human-facing artefacts — macro/per-class F1, confusion matrix, reliability diagram, ECE, sector/year stability — let an ML engineer audit a classifier; none of them let a PM see why a given call was scored negative. The one genuinely inspectable idea in the plan (LM tone as a benchmark) is relegated to an ablation rung rather than being the deliverable.
issues.what_breaks: The Validation section. Even a clean positive result arrives as a residual score with no traceable path from a sentence a manager said to a position decision, so the IC cannot approve acting on it.
issues.fix: Invert the ladder: make the dictionary/rule-based Q&A tone measure the primary specification, and require, as a deliverable, ten calls traced end to end — the flagged sentences, the hedging phrases, the evasion instances, the peer comparison, and the subsequent 3-12 month outcome — that a PM can read and agree or disagree with.

issues.summary: Months of pretraining, annotation and infrastructure are committed before the cheap test that could kill the idea.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The single most decisive question — does any peer-relative tone deviation survive controls for SUE and the 3-day announcement return — is answerable with Loughran-McDonald counts, which the plan already builds as a benchmark, on a few thousand calls. Instead LM tone appears only as ablation rung one, downstream of ~2B tokens of MLM pretraining, a 6,000-sentence gold set, and 150k silver labels. If the dictionary version is flat, the entire transformer stack was wasted; if it is strong, the firm may not need the transformer at all.
issues.what_breaks: The Methodology ordering. First usable output arrives at the end, after the largest irreversible spend, and there is no stated point at which the project stops.
issues.fix: Run the dictionary-only version on Q&A versus prepared remarks with peer demeaning and the SUE/announcement-return controls first, on a 2015-2020 subsample. Pre-commit: if peer-relative dictionary tone shows no monotone quintile spread and no sign consistency across the three peer definitions, stop and write the null up in week two.

issues.summary: Incrementality is established against FinBERT, not against the published tone signals already in systematic books.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Call-tone, Q&A-versus-prepared, hedging/uncertainty and managerial-evasion signals are among the most heavily published equity NLP results, and the plan cites Cao-Jiang-Wang-Yang itself. The ablation ladder shows lift over LM and FinBERT — i.e. over weaker measurement — but never asks whether the surviving residual is orthogonal to what is already crowded. Crowding is acknowledged only through the cost/break-even channel, which is a different question from whether the return was already arbitraged.
issues.what_breaks: Interpretation of the Validation ablation. A positive result could be a rediscovery with better measurement error, which is not a tradeable edge for a late entrant.
issues.fix: Add one cheap step before building anything: reproduce two or three published call-tone results on the 2015-2020 sample and check whether the reported effect still exists post-2018. If the published version is dead, that is the finding and it costs a week.

issues.summary: The firm's own most relevant evidence — a decade of calls on names it has owned and been right or wrong about — is not used.
issues.why_it_applies_here: For a concentrated Type-I-dominant book, the judgeable question is whether tone deviation would have flagged the specific business deteriorations this firm actually suffered. The plan instead manufactures Russell 3000 cross-sectional N to reach a factor t-stat, which is the right design for a quant shop and the wrong one for deciding whether an analyst should weight Q&A tone in a fundamental case.
issues.what_breaks: The output is a portfolio alpha rather than an answer to 'should we read Q&A this way on our names.' Even a t>3 result leaves the PM without a usable rule.
issues.fix: Add a within-portfolio retrospective: for every position exited at a loss and every large peer-relative drawdown in the last ten years, was there a detectable Q&A tone or evasion deviation one to four quarters before? Consistency across those cases is real evidence here even without cross-sectional significance.

result.overall: As a piece of quantitative research design this is unusually careful — pre-registered primary specification, single-touch holdout, an explicit null, a placebo, three peer definitions, break-even cost as a first-class result, and named failure modes including t-stat hunting. The problem is that it was written for a different firm: a systematic shop with engineers, a factor book, and a monthly rebalance. For a five-person Bloomberg-and-Excel long-only manager holding 25-30 names for three to five years, it is unexecutable, produces a long-short object they cannot trade at a horizon they cannot use, and delivers a score their IC cannot inspect. Send it back with the horizon changed to fundamental deterioration over 12-24 months, the primary measure changed to something an analyst can hand-check, and a two-week dictionary-based kill test on their own names run before any spend.

result.plan_implied_asker: A systematic equity quant shop with WRDS/CRSP infrastructure, a decile long-short book, and researchers fluent in asset-pricing econometrics
