result.what_would_falsify: Explicit and pre-committed: tone t below 2.5 (2.9 Bonferroni with three variants); net long-short spread under 3% annualised or IR under 0.4; correct sign in fewer than 7 of 10 years; spread concentrated in the bottom size quintile; a non-zero placebo coefficient over [-63,-3]; failure of the shuffled-speaker-label control; rank correlation above 0.7 with a vendor score meaning the signal is commodity. A t of 2.1 is stated as a kill.

issues.summary: The data assembly is a database-engineering project this firm has no capacity to execute.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan requires WRDS-hosted Capital IQ transcripts with publication timestamps, point-in-time CRSP with delisting returns, Compustat with reporting lag, I/B/E/S SUE and Guidance files, point-in-time GICS sub-industry, and Hoberg-Phillips TNIC-3, joined across ~90,000 firm-quarters, with speaker-tag parsing of every transcript. The firm's stated tooling is Bloomberg, Excel and filings, with no engineers, no data scientists and nobody who maintains a database.
issues.what_breaks: Days 4-10 never happen. There is no environment in which two-way clustered panel regressions on a point-in-time merged panel get run by one analyst in Excel, so every downstream gate, kill criterion and validation step is unreachable.
issues.fix: Either buy the study (commission an academic or a vendor to run the pre-registered specification and deliver tables) or replace it with the hand-executable version: pull Q&A transcripts for the 30 held names plus a 40-name watchlist off Bloomberg, hand-code or LM-score tone in Excel across the last 20 quarters, and test within-name whether tone deterioration preceded peer-relative underperformance.

issues.summary: The pass branch and two of the four kill criteria describe a product this firm cannot trade, which means the study both rejects findings it could use and accepts findings it cannot.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Kill criterion (2) requires a 3% net annualised spread and IR 0.4 from a monthly-rebalanced decile long-short with overlapping 60-day tranches; the pass branch is scoping 'infrastructure, latency, capacity'. This firm runs 25-30 long positions for three to five years, cannot short, cannot rebalance monthly, and latency and capacity are not concepts that bear on it. Conversely, the finding that would matter to them — that a within-firm tone deterioration is an early flag that a business they own is turning — is not tested anywhere and would be killed by failing criterion (2).
issues.what_breaks: The day-10 portfolio step and the all-four gate. A real, decision-relevant effect gets discarded for failing a portfolio test that is irrelevant here, and a passing result routes to a build the firm cannot staff.
issues.fix: Drop the long-short spread, IR, latency and capacity work entirely. Replace criterion (2) with the usable-form test: conditional on a large negative within-firm tone change, what is the distribution of peer-relative return, the hit rate, and how often did it coincide with a subsequent guidance cut or estimate revision cycle — a diagnostic a fundamental analyst can act on inside an existing position.

issues.summary: The 2004-2010 replication and the decay-curve estimation cannot be run on the stated sample.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The data section specifies calls from January 2015 to the latest complete quarter. Days 6-7 require replicating 2004-2010 with a t near 3, and the day-2 work commits to 'estimate the decay curve directly'. The sample contains none of the pre-2015 period on which both rest.
issues.what_breaks: The plan's central framing — real in 2004-2010, arbitraged since — becomes an assumption rather than a result, and the McLean-Pontiff one-third prior is imported instead of measured. A weak post-2015 coefficient then cannot be distinguished from a signal that never worked at all.
issues.fix: Either license transcripts back to 2004 (and price that before committing) or delete the replication and the decay curve, and state plainly that the design tests only whether the effect is present now.

issues.summary: Nothing in the output is inspectable by an investment committee skeptical of models it cannot inspect.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The deliverables are a pooled panel with industry-by-quarter fixed effects, two-way clustered errors, Fama-MacBeth with Newey-West lags, FF5 plus momentum plus reversal attribution, and a Bonferroni-adjusted t threshold. There is no worked example, no distribution of the tone measure, no hand-read transcript traced from text to score to signal to outcome. The only human-inspectable artefact mentioned is extreme-decile sector composition, buried in the pitfalls list.
issues.what_breaks: Even if the study passes its gate, the IC cannot verify it and will not fund action on it. The fourteen days produce a number the audience has to take on faith.
issues.fix: Add on day 5, before any regression: the histogram of the within-firm tone change, coverage and missingness by quarter, and ten transcripts hand-read by the analyst with the computed score alongside their own read. Then present the headline result as a simple contingency table — top-decile versus bottom-decile tone change, hit rate against peers by year — with the clustered regression as an appendix rather than the exhibit.

issues.summary: A 63-day peer-relative return horizon is the wrong horizon for a three-to-five-year book, and the plan never tests the horizon that matters here.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The signal is measured over [+2,+63] and gated on next-quarter performance because that is the horizon in the anchor literature. What kills this firm is being wrong about a business over years. Whether a management tone shift foreshadows a multi-year deterioration in fundamentals is a different question from whether it predicts one quarter of relative return, and the second answer does not imply the first.
issues.what_breaks: Days 4-10 and the gate. A passing quarterly t leaves the firm with a signal whose economic life is shorter than its rebalancing tolerance; a failing quarterly t does not license the conclusion that tone is uninformative about business trajectory.
issues.fix: Add [+2,+252] and [+2,+756] peer-relative return as co-primary horizons, and add a fundamental outcome — subsequent four-quarter revision to consensus EPS or realised margin path — so a null on price still yields a usable answer about whether tone leads the business.

issues.summary: Management turnover and Q&A composition will mechanically move the within-firm differenced tone measure.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The signal is defined as the change in LM net tone versus the prior four calls, which is exactly what a change of CEO or CFO produces — a new speaker's habitual vocabulary shifts net tone with no change in sentiment about the business. Management turnover is itself predictive of subsequent relative returns, so this is a confound that will generate a coefficient with the right sign for the wrong reason. Denominator sensitivity compounds it: normalising by total Q&A words means a quarter with more or longer analyst questions changes the measure without any change in what was said.
issues.what_breaks: The primary regression's tone coefficient is contaminated, and no listed control (size, B/M, momentum, dispersion, prior-quarter tone level) absorbs it. The shuffled-speaker-label placebo does not catch it either, since shuffling mixes in analyst text and will attenuate the signal almost mechanically.
issues.fix: Add a same-speaker restriction or a speaker-change indicator interacted with tone, and report the result on the subsample with no CEO/CFO change in the trailing five calls. Report tone per answer and per sentence alongside the words-normalised version.

issues.summary: The question can be killed for free in two days, before any data spend.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan already contains the cheap kill and then walks past it. The day-2 vendor calls establish that point-in-time earnings-call tone scores are commercially available to 2010 from at least eight providers with substantial client counts, and the plan itself treats availability as evidence of crowding. If a one-month S&P Global or MarketPsych trial shows their score has no incremental power to SUE, CAR and guidance in a simple Bloomberg-and-Excel cut on a few hundred names, the answer for this firm is settled without WRDS, without CRSP, and without fourteen days.
issues.what_breaks: Ordering, and the spend committed before the premise is tested. The most entropy-reducing step per dollar is the vendor trial, and it currently sits in the validation section behind the whole build.
issues.fix: Move the vendor trial to days 1-3. Score the 400 largest Russell names for the last eight quarters against Bloomberg total-return-versus-sector data in Excel. If the incremental sign is absent or wrong there, write the negative memo and stop.

result.overall: The research design itself is unusually disciplined — a frozen pre-registration, an explicit expected null, a decay prior, four pre-committed kill criteria, real placebos, and an honest treatment of LLM look-ahead and vendor crowding. It is also written for a firm that does not exist here: it assumes WRDS, CRSP, Compustat, I/B/E/S and transcript parsing across 90,000 firm-quarters, delivers a monthly-rebalanced long-short with latency and capacity scoping, and gates on econometrics an IC that distrusts uninspectable models cannot check. Send it back with the infrastructure and portfolio machinery deleted, the horizon extended to one and three years, and the vendor trial moved to day one — that version can be executed by one analyst in Excel and can kill the idea in a week.

result.plan_implied_asker: Mid-frequency systematic equity fund with WRDS/TAQ infrastructure, a quant research team, and daily-rebalance execution capability
result.what_would_falsify: Stated and specific: if RLOIB's incremental Fama-MacBeth coefficient controlling for ALLOIB and RETOIB has |t|<2.0 at every horizon, the lot filter adds nothing; if it survives but net-of-cost long-short alpha has t<3.0 under base costs, the effect is real but unharvestable. The weakness is the 'at every horizon' construction combined with a large sensitivity grid, which makes the kill nearly impossible to trigger.

issues.summary: The entire design is a daily-rebalanced systematic long-short study for a firm with no engineers, no database, and a three-to-five-year holding period.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Executing this specific plan requires cleaning NYSE Daily TAQ trade-and-quote data from 2015 to present per Holden-Jacobsen, building four separately-constructed signed imbalance measures, running rolling 250-day residualizations, daily decile sorts with 5-day overlapping holding periods, and a square-root impact model with participation caps. That is a multi-person quant data engineering stack. The stated tooling is Bloomberg, Excel and filings, with one operations person and nobody maintaining a database. Even if the research were correct, the resulting strategy turns the book over every one to five days against a mandate of 25-30 positions held three to five years.
issues.what_breaks: The data step fails before any result exists; and if it somehow completed, the tradeable output (a value-weighted, beta-neutral, borrow-fee-constrained decile long-short refreshed daily) is not a product this firm can hold, finance, or explain to allocators.
issues.fix: Kill the plan as written. If the underlying curiosity matters, restate it as a question this firm can act on: does retail flow concentration in our 25-30 names tell us anything about entry timing or price fragility over quarters, using a purchased retail-flow indicator on Bloomberg rather than reconstructing it from TAQ.

issues.summary: No statement of what is incremental: retail order-flow imbalance and its short-horizon reversal are published, productized, and heavily traded, and the plan never asks whether the round-lot version is anything but a worse instrument for a crowded signal.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's own construction concedes the point: it builds RETOIB from subpenny off-exchange prints, which is the standard published retail identifier, and then asks whether RLOIB adds anything on top. It never says why a 100-share-multiple filter would be a better retail instrument than the subpenny classifier — and a priori it is worse, since round-lot multiples are the canonical footprint of institutional algo slicing while retail is disproportionately odd-lot and, post-2019, fractional. So the best realistic outcome is a small increment on a measure whose historical Sharpe is already in wholesalers' and quant funds' books. Nothing in the plan addresses crowding or post-2021 decay in retail-flow signals.
issues.what_breaks: The evaluation step regresses net returns on in-house ALLOIB/RETOIB factors and asks for t>3.0 — but even a pass is a claim of increment over a signal whose baseline availability going forward is unexamined. A pass gets read as an edge when it is most likely a rediscovery.
issues.fix: Before any data work, write one page: who currently trades retail-flow reversal, at what horizon, at what capacity, and what has happened to its performance since 2021. If the answer is that the base signal is crowded and decayed, the round-lot increment is not worth the pipeline regardless of its t-statistic.

issues.summary: The output cannot be inspected or defended to an investment committee that is explicitly skeptical of models it cannot check.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The mandate states the deliverable must be defensible to a skeptical IC. What this plan delivers is a residualized, winsorized, cross-sectionally z-scored imbalance measure, a Fama-MacBeth coefficient with Newey-West(h+5) errors cross-checked against Hansen-Hodrick and a block bootstrap, and a net alpha against nine factors including two in-house ones. There is no worked example an analyst could trace by hand, no hand-checked sample of classified prints, no distribution of RLOIB by price bucket shown early, no coverage-by-year table. Lee-Ready signing errors and TAQ condition-code choices are exactly the places this breaks silently, and nothing in the plan surfaces them for human eyes.
issues.what_breaks: Every intermediate stage is opaque until the final alpha table, so a bad branch (e.g. sale conditions reintroducing auction volume, or a PERMNO mapping break across corporate actions) is only discoverable after the whole pipeline is sunk — and the IC has no basis to accept or reject the number when it arrives.
issues.fix: If any version proceeds, require in week one: hand-traced signing for 50 prints in 5 names, RLOIB distribution by price decile and by year, round-lot share of volume by year, and print/volume coverage by year — all inspectable in Excel — before a single regression is run.

issues.summary: 'Round lot' does not mean the same thing across the sample, and it changes meaning precisely at the 2019 split point used for out-of-sample validation.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan holds the 100-share threshold fixed and notes the Dec 2013 odd-lot reporting break and the later SEC tiering. It does not address that zero-commission and dollar-based/fractional investing after late 2019 shifted retail order sizes away from round multiples, and that wholesaler internalization conventions changed over the same window. The train/test split is placed at end-2019 — the same date as the measurement regime change.
issues.what_breaks: The validation step cannot distinguish signal decay from a change in what the measure captures, so a post-2019 failure is uninterpretable and a post-2019 success is suspect. The 2021 stress-test window sits entirely in the regime where the retail-to-round-lot link is weakest.
issues.fix: Report round-lot share of volume, and the RLOIB-RETOIB rolling correlation, year by year as a first-order diagnostic. If that correlation collapses after 2019, the measure is answering a different question in each half and the split-sample design is void.

issues.summary: The kill criterion is written so it almost cannot fire: failure requires |t|<2.0 at every horizon, across a signing/scaling/weighting/smoothing sensitivity grid and multiple signal variants.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan tests h=1, 5 and 20, on raw and residual signals, with a 'retail-plausible' 100-500 share variant and an exact-100 bucket, across a sensitivity grid over signing algorithm, NBBO lag, scaling, smoothing, earnings inclusion, deciles versus quintiles, weighting and impact calibration. Under that many draws, at least one |t|>2.0 is close to guaranteed under the null, and the plan pre-commits to reinterpreting rather than rejecting a horizon sign flip ('a positive 20-day coefficient is reinterpreted, not failure').
issues.what_breaks: The stated falsifier stops functioning as a falsifier at the identification stage; only the net-alpha t>3.0 gate remains binding, and the plan will arrive there having already accumulated a narrative.
issues.fix: Pre-register one primary specification and one primary horizon before looking, with the grid as post-hoc robustness only, and state the sign the mechanism predicts at each horizon in advance.

issues.summary: The determinative and near-free check sits behind the most expensive step; licences and analyst weeks are committed before anything cheap has been learned.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Whether a round-lot filter tracks retail at all is a question answerable from published work and a vendor retail-flow indicator in under a day. Instead the plan requires full WRDS TAQ access, IHS Markit or Ortex lending fees, and Refinitiv 13F before the RLOIB-RETOIB correlation — the check that determines whether the rest is worth doing — is ever computed. For a $400M shop that buys data occasionally and cannot operate infrastructure, that ordering commits real spend against a premise that could be tested for nothing.
issues.what_breaks: Weeks of the firm's only spare analyst capacity and several data licences are spent before the first entropy-reducing result, on a question that has a one-day answer.
issues.fix: Sequence: (1) read the retail-flow literature and note which lot-size and print-type conventions identify retail; (2) get any off-the-shelf retail-flow series and correlate it with a crude Bloomberg round-lot proxy; (3) only if that link is strong and the base signal is not visibly decayed, consider whether this firm should be in this business at all.

result.overall: This is a competently constructed microstructure study — the falsifier is explicit, the cost model is honest, the placebos are real — written for the wrong firm and, most likely, for a question that is already answered and already traded. A five-person Bloomberg-and-Excel long-only shop with three-to-five-year holds cannot build the TAQ pipeline, cannot run a daily-rebalanced decile long-short, and cannot defend the resulting number to its own IC; and the plan never establishes why a round-lot filter would be a better retail instrument than the subpenny classifier that the market has already monetized. Kill it in a day with the reading-plus-vendor-correlation check, and if retail flow is genuinely interesting here, reframe it as a price-fragility diagnostic on the 25-30 names they actually own.

result.plan_implied_asker: A systematic microstructure/short-horizon quant desk with TAQ licences, engineers, and intraday execution capability
result.what_would_falsify: Pre-committed kills: retail lift <2.0x (or bootstrap LB <1.5x), recall <35%, signing accuracy <70%, stock-day correlation with the sub-penny benchmark <0.40 (or VandaTrack <0.25), and |t|<3 on round-lot imbalance once sub-penny retail imbalance is in the same forward-return regression. H0 is stated affirmatively with a mechanism (fractional/dollar orders arrive odd-lot; VWAP/TWAP schedulers slice into 100-share children), so round lots become an institutional signature.

issues.summary: The plan is written for a firm with data engineering; this firm has five people, no engineers, and Bloomberg/Excel/filings.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Phase 1 as specified requires 36 months of NYSE Daily TAQ trades plus NBBO at nanosecond stamps (multi-terabyte), partitioned Parquet with DuckDB/Spark, historical proprietary exchange feeds carrying RLP flags from seven venues, Lee-Ready signing with lag-robustness checks, and CRSP linkage. One analyst with Excel cannot build or maintain that, and nobody here maintains a database. The licence and storage spend is committed before anything actionable exists.
issues.what_breaks: Everything after Benchmark C. G1-G5 are all TAQ- or proprietary-feed-dependent, so the entire gate structure is unexecutable and the project stalls after the spreadsheet step, having already paid for data.
issues.fix: Stop the plan at Benchmark C (Rule 605 wholesaler reports by odd-lot/fractional/dollar bucket plus FINRA OTC transparency by MPID). That is spreadsheet-only, and the plan itself concedes it alone can kill the project. If C does not kill it, buy the answer as a research note rather than building the pipeline.

issues.summary: Even a clean pass on H1 and Phase 2 produces a strategy this firm cannot trade, so the work has no path to a decision.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The only edge available in retail-flow identification is speed and order-routing access. The counterparties are the internalizers named in the plan's own Benchmark C list — Citadel, Virtu, Jane Street — whose core business is paying for exactly this flow because it is identifiable. A 25-30 position long-only book with no execution infrastructure has neither the latency nor the routing to monetize an intraday imbalance signal, and the plan never states what would be incremental to what those firms already extract.
issues.what_breaks: The Phase 2 go/no-go (after-cost Sharpe ≥1.0, net/gross >0.40) is defined against an implementation this firm cannot run, so the gate cannot be evaluated and a pass would be unusable.
issues.fix: Answer the firm-fit question first, in a one-page memo: if H1 passed tomorrow, what would we do differently in this book? If the answer is nothing, kill now. If the intended use is execution quality on our own orders rather than trading against retail, reframe the question to that.

issues.summary: Signal horizon is minutes-to-days; the book holds three to five years.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Round-lot imbalance and retail order-flow continuation are microstructure effects measured off nanosecond timestamps with Lee-Ready signing at 1ms lag; the Phase 2 test is directional continuation and spread-capture economics. Nothing in that persists over a three-to-five-year hold, and the risk this firm actually loses money on is being wrong about a business.
issues.what_breaks: The horizon of the deliverable and the horizon of the portfolio never intersect, so no Phase 1 or Phase 2 result changes a position.
issues.fix: Redirect the analyst time to a question at the book's horizon, or explicitly reposition this as vendor due diligence on a retail-flow dataset someone else would trade.

issues.summary: Hui-Walter latent-class estimation, Lee-Ready signing, double-clustered panel SEs and Benjamini-Hochberg cannot be inspected by an IC that is explicitly skeptical of models it cannot inspect.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The IC's stated bar is inspectability. The central identification claim — the ≥2x lift — rests on a latent-class estimator whose whole purpose is to correct for label error the committee cannot see, and the kill threshold sits on its bootstrap lower bound. There is no simple corroborating cut the committee could verify by hand.
issues.what_breaks: G1. Whatever it returns, the committee cannot distinguish a real 2.1x lift from an artifact of the latent-class specification, so the number carries no decision.
issues.fix: Pair every gate with a check a person can read off a table: raw round-lot share of RLP-flagged executions versus raw round-lot share of all executions, by venue and size quintile, with counts shown. If the crude version does not show the lift, the latent-class version should not be trusted to manufacture it.

issues.summary: The sub-penny benchmark is used both to define the retail partition and to validate round lots against, making G4 and G5 partly circular.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The venue partitioning step splits off-exchange volume by NBBO position and sub-penny improvement, and G4/G5 then score round-lot imbalance against Benchmark A, which is the sub-penny rule. Within the sub-penny-improved partition the label and the partition share the same construction, so agreement is partly definitional rather than evidence that round lots carry retail content.
issues.what_breaks: G4's r≥0.40 and G5's |t|≥3 can pass inside the sub-penny partition for mechanical reasons, and that is the partition most likely to be the one that passes, triggering Phase 2 on a definitional result.
issues.fix: Require the passing partition to be one where the validating label is independent of the partitioning variable — RLP-flagged lit executions for G3/G4 — and treat sub-penny-partition agreement as descriptive only.

issues.summary: The sample is deliberately confined to the pre-half-penny, fixed-100 regime, which is the regime that no longer exists.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Benchmark A is stated to be valid only before half-penny compliance, and round-lot status is being redefined on a tiered 100/40/10/1 basis. Both breaks land exactly in the period a signal would trade. The plan computes round-lot status under both definitions but tests only in the old regime, so the thing being measured changes meaning across the boundary the conclusion needs to cross.
issues.what_breaks: A pass on G1-G5 licenses Phase 2 in a microstructure that has already been replaced; a fail could be an artifact of the old definition rather than evidence about the new one.
issues.fix: State up front that the deliverable is a historical-regime finding with unknown forward validity, and add a small post-compliance descriptive cut (round-lot share by tier and venue) before any Phase 2 commitment.

result.overall: As a piece of research design this is unusually good — it separates identification from profitability, states H0 affirmatively with a real mechanism, pre-commits kill thresholds, and puts the cheapest killing test first. It is written for the wrong firm: TAQ plus Spark plus historical proprietary feeds is unbuildable here, the latent-class machinery is uninspectable by this IC, the horizon is minutes against a three-to-five-year book, and even a clean pass yields a strategy that competes with the internalizers who buy this flow and that this desk cannot execute. Run Benchmark C alone — Rule 605 buckets plus FINRA OTC transparency, a week in Excel — and write the one-page note on what we would do differently if H1 held; the honest expected outcome is a fast, well-evidenced kill with no data spend.

result.plan_implied_asker: A concentrated fundamental long-only or event-driven shop holding one name for multiple years, with forensic-accounting analysts and an investment committee
result.what_would_falsify: Stated and genuine: negative implied gross bookings two consecutive quarters; channel inventory >1.5x normal; a backlog/LTA definition change in a quarter that would otherwise have declined; supplier finished-goods inventory rising two quarters while backlog is called record; customer mirror disclosures reconciling to <~50% of announced commitments.

issues.summary: This is a multi-year single-name fundamental durability study delivered to a systematic firm that trades a days-to-weeks horizon on cross-sectionally replicable signals.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The output is a coverage ratio, an EV/haircut-adjusted committed gross profit comparison and a reverse DCF on one issuer's 3-year agreements against a 10-15 year depreciation schedule. Nothing in that is a signal the research platform can re-run across a universe, and the firm's stated pass/fail criteria (survives transaction costs, has capacity, is not crowded) cannot even be computed from it. A firm with 200 researchers and 20 years of transcripts asking 'does shortage guidance portend durable revenue' is asking whether the event class is tradable, not for a forensic file on one name.
issues.what_breaks: The entire methodology section — bridge, register, scenarios, reverse DCF — produces an artifact that has no consumer at this firm. Even if every number is right, no position can be sized from it and the committee has nothing to replicate.
issues.fix: Reframe as an event study: extract shortage/'sold out'/extended-lead-time guidance language from the full transcript history, and test cross-sectionally (a) whether announced LTA value and RPO step up in the following 2-4 quarters, (b) whether forward revenue dispersion actually falls versus matched non-shortage-guiding peers, and (c) abnormal returns at 1/5/20/60 days with costs. Keep the single-name file only as a worked example that validates the automated tagging.

issues.summary: Analysis horizon (8 quarters forward, 3-year agreements, 10-15 year depreciation, market-implied durable horizon in years) is one to two orders of magnitude longer than the book's holding period.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The specific tests chosen — capex carried into a 10-15 year depreciation schedule, 'modeled horizon exceeding market-implied by ≥2 years', year-two coverage ≥40% — only pay off if the position is held through the resolution of the shortage cycle. On a days-to-weeks horizon what matters is the repricing that follows the disclosure of committed volume (the 8-K, the RPO print, the customer purchase-obligation table), not whether the commitment ultimately converts in 2027.
issues.what_breaks: The threshold set gates on quantities that cannot resolve inside the holding period, so the signal is never actionable; the scenario tree (2Q early / on guidance / 4Q late) is resolution-path analysis for a holder, not a trader.
issues.fix: Re-anchor on the disclosure calendar: which filing or event reveals commitment quality, how much of the mispricing corrects within 5-20 trading days of it, and whether the surprise component is measurable before the print. Drop the depreciation schedule and the 2-year horizon gap entirely.

issues.summary: The one cheap test that determines whether anything else is worth doing — do prior shortage-guidance episodes actually show an LTA/RPO step-up and abnormal forward returns — is scheduled last, under 'Validation'.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's own pitfalls section concedes that shortage guidance induces the agreement-signing being measured and that announcement count carries no information. That makes the historical episode scan the premise test, not a robustness layer: if the 2017-18 and 2021-22 cohorts show that coverage step-ups did not predict lower realized revenue variance or positive forward returns, the bridge, register, six-attribute scoring, scenario tree and reverse DCF are all wasted. At this firm that scan is days of work, not weeks.
issues.what_breaks: Weeks of hand-built accounting reconstruction are sunk before the premise is tested, and the first inspectable output arrives only after the register and bridge are complete.
issues.fix: Run the episode scan first as a standalone kill gate with a pre-committed pass condition (e.g. realized revenue dispersion in the two years after shortage guidance must be materially below the pre-period and below matched peers, in a majority of episodes). Only build the register if it passes.

issues.summary: The RPO roll-forward solves net bookings as a plug and then backs cancellations out of book-to-bill, so the 'negative implied gross bookings' kill trigger is a residual that absorbs every disclosure artifact.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Companies restate RPO for definitional changes, adopt practical expedients, exclude unbilled non-cancelable amounts inconsistently, and fold in M&A and FX with no disclosure granularity. The plan already knows this — it plans to footnote restatements — yet it then interprets the sign of the plug as economic content ('hidden cancellations') and elevates it to one of only two hard quantitative negative triggers. Backing cancellations out of book-to-bill compounds it, since book-to-bill is computed from the bookings figure that was itself solved as a plug.
issues.what_breaks: The bridge's headline diagnostic and one of the kill criteria are unidentified: a definitional restatement or an acquisition can flip the sign either way, so the trigger fires on noise or fails to fire on real cancellations.
issues.fix: Bound the plug before interpreting it — reconstruct the same roll-forward on 20-30 firm-quarters where cancellations or restatements are separately disclosed, and report the distribution of the residual when nothing economic happened. If that distribution straddles zero materially, drop 'negative implied gross bookings' as a trigger and replace it with the customer-side purchase-obligation mirror check, which is directly observed.

issues.summary: Roughly a dozen hand-set parameters — tier haircuts of 90-95/70/25-35%, and six pass thresholds plus four negative triggers — are calibrated on one prior episode and never tested out of sample as a set.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The haircuts are said to be calibrated from 2021-23 semiconductor realized conversion, but they then feed an EV/haircut-adjusted committed gross profit comparison and a horizon gap that drives the verdict. One cycle, one industry, with the tier boundaries drawn after seeing the outcomes, is not enough to pin a 70% versus 25% conversion rate — and the difference between those two numbers decides the answer. The threshold list ('constructive requires all of', six conditions) has the same problem: it looks like it was written to describe cases already known to have worked.
issues.what_breaks: Coverage, the EV comparison, and the constructive/negative verdict are all functions of parameters with wide unacknowledged uncertainty; the plan will produce a confident tier-weighted number whose sensitivity to the haircuts is never shown.
issues.fix: Fit haircuts on one episode cohort and report realized conversion out of sample on a different one (memory 2017-18, telecom 2000). Show the verdict's sensitivity to the tier weights. Replace the conjunctive 'all of' gate with a scored composite so that near-misses are visible rather than discarded.

issues.summary: Nothing in the plan addresses the three things this firm uses to judge work: transaction costs, capacity, and crowding.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Shortage-guidance and 'record backlog' language is exactly the kind of narrative that sell-side and systematic NLP factor books have already mined; supply-chain and guidance-language sentiment factors are widely commercialized. The plan's only nod to what the market believes is a reverse DCF on one name's implied durable horizon, which says nothing about whether the event class is already in everyone's book. Capacity also bites specifically: shortage-guiding names in a bottleneck cycle are a small, correlated, frequently hard-to-borrow set.
issues.what_breaks: Even a correct fundamental conclusion cannot be promoted to production, and the committee's first question has no answer.
issues.fix: Add, to the reframed event study, decile turnover and cost-adjusted returns, the borrow/ADV profile of the event cohort, and a check of whether the effect has decayed across the four episode cohorts chronologically — decay across cohorts is the crowding read.

issues.summary: The core input — a six-attribute judgment score on each agreement plus adversarial transcript reading — is not codified, so the research committee cannot independently reproduce it.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This firm's stated standard is that any result is replicated on the research platform before it trades. 'Minimum quantities vs. best-efforts', 'reschedulable within a lead-time window' and 'term drift' are analyst reads of contract language; two researchers will tier the same 8-K differently, and the tier assignment is what moves coverage from 90% to 30%.
issues.what_breaks: The replication step fails not because the result is wrong but because the input is not reproducible, and the plan surfaces no inter-rater check to show how much of the answer is scorer-dependent.
issues.fix: Codify the six attributes as extraction rules over filing text with a labelled gold set, report agreement between two independent scorers on 50 agreements, and publish the confusion between Tier 2 and Tier 3 — that boundary carries most of the variance in the conclusion.

issues.summary: EV/haircut-adjusted committed gross profit on a 'normalized margin' compares a shortage-peak name to peers and to its own history, where the multiple means different things.
issues.why_it_applies_here: During a shortage the committed dollars carry peak price and peak margin; after resolution the same volume carries rolled-off pricing, which the plan's own early-resolution scenario acknowledges. Choosing the normalized margin therefore determines the entire cross-time and cross-peer comparison, and peers in the same episode are contaminated by the same peak. The plan names the pricing-rolloff risk in the scenarios but does not carry it into the multiple.
issues.what_breaks: The valuation leg — 'current EV does not already price that' — becomes a function of an unstated margin assumption rather than of the commitment structure the analysis was built to measure.
issues.fix: Split coverage into quantity and price legs (the plan already does this) and quote the multiple on quantity coverage at trough-cycle margin as the base case, showing peak-margin as an upside variant rather than the headline.

result.overall: The fundamental craft here is genuinely good — separating RPO from company-defined backlog from announced LTA value, insisting that announcement count is uninformative, the customer-mirror reconciliation, the enforcement-is-an-upper-bound point, and the duration-versus-growth downgrade are all things a strong analyst gets right and most miss. But it is written for the wrong firm and the wrong question: it is a multi-year forensic file on one issuer, with a reverse DCF and a 10-15 year depreciation schedule, handed to a systematic desk that trades days to weeks and promotes nothing it cannot replicate, cost, and capacity-test across a universe. The premise test is also last: for a fraction of this cost the firm could scan every shortage-guidance transcript in its history, measure whether committed volume actually steps up, whether realized revenue dispersion actually falls, and whether the market already pays for it — a week of work that either kills the idea or tells you what the single-name file should look for.

result.plan_implied_asker: A concentrated fundamental long-only or event-driven fund with multi-year holding periods and a contract-analyst bench
result.what_would_falsify: Episodes where contracted price stayed materially above spot for 8+ quarters after supply normalization, absent a hard qualification moat — plus the pre-registered HBM checks (contract-liability direction, RPO growth threshold, customs shipments, customer obligation-table growth) and the requirement that aerospace/LNG score durable while MLCC/containers score fragile when ordered by qualification lag rather than contract label.

issues.summary: The deliverable — a hand-coded, discretionary multiple haircut on one name — is not something this firm can trade or its committee can re-run.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Work here is judged on surviving transaction costs, capacity and crowding, and the research platform replicates any result before it trades. Steps 2 and 3 rest on one analyst's ordinal judgment of Exhibit 10 language across 20-30 episodes in ten industries; there is no restatement path for a second researcher to reproduce that coding, and no cost, capacity or crowding analysis anywhere in the plan. The output ('a probability-weighted haircut, not a verdict') is a discretionary fundamental opinion.
issues.what_breaks: Validation stage. Even if the framework is correct, the committee cannot independently reproduce the ordinal outcome codes, so nothing gets to production; the firm's actual comparative advantage — tick data, full EDGAR history, hundreds of events — is unused.
issues.fix: Recast the primary deliverable as a machine-reproducible cross-sectional event study: EDGAR full-text search for allocation/LTA/take-or-pay language across all filers 2005-2025 (the plan already builds this in step 1), returns measured at the firm's horizon around both the signature disclosure and the unwind disclosure, with cost and capacity attached. Keep the 20-30 hand-coded episodes as the mechanism narrative that explains and constrains the machine signal, not as the primary evidence.

issues.summary: Outcomes are coded at T+4/8/12 quarters and the falsifier requires 8+ quarters of post-normalization pricing, against a book that holds positions days to weeks.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Even taking the hypothesis as proven — LTAs hold in volume and break in price two to four quarters after overhang lands — the tradeable information is the disclosure event, not the eventual repricing. The plan's measurement clock is two to three years long; the firm's is two to three weeks. Nothing in the design identifies when the market learns of the unwind, which is the only moment a days-to-weeks book can act.
issues.what_breaks: Step 3 and the falsifier. The study can conclude correctly and still hand the PM nothing to put on, because the repricing is realized over quarters and the plan never locates the disclosure moment that reprices the stock.
issues.fix: Add an explicit event calendar of unwind-revealing disclosures — contract-liability reversals, RPO declines, purchase-obligation-table cuts, guidance language shifts — and measure returns in the days-to-weeks window around each. That converts a multi-year fundamental truth into a horizon-matched signal or shows there isn't one.

issues.summary: The premise that the market prices disclosed LTA books as a duration story deserving a higher multiple is inherited from the question and never tested, despite being the cheapest and most decisive check available.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The entire economic case is that consensus over-credits LTA duration and this work is variant. But 'read by the market as a duration story' is asserted in the first sentence and appears nowhere in the method. The polysilicon-take-or-pay-collapse and container-rate-abandonment narratives are well-worn sell-side material; if disclosure of a large LTA book is already discounted, the variant view is not variant and there is no money in it regardless of how well the contract coding is done.
issues.what_breaks: The premise sits upstream of everything. If LTA-book disclosure carries no positive multiple response, steps 2-6 answer a question with no trade attached, and the three months of contract coding is sunk.
issues.fix: Run this first, in a week, with the firm's own data: measure the price and multiple response to RPO/contract-liability/purchase-obligation-table increases in shortage regimes, and the response to their reversals. If the signature is not rewarded, or the reversal is already anticipated, kill the project there. If it is rewarded and reversals surprise, the rest of the plan is justified.

issues.summary: The 2021-2024 auto-semi holdout is not blind — its outcome is already described in the plan's own episode list.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The validation section proposes building the framework on everything else and predicting auto-semi outcomes 'before checking,' but the episode list already states onsemi's ~$16bn committed LTSA volume and Renesas's ~$2bn Wolfspeed deposit 'through the 2023-2025 correction.' The analyst knows the answer, so the holdout tests recall, not the framework.
issues.what_breaks: The out-of-sample claim. The framework will appear to generalize when it has been fit to a known outcome, inflating confidence in the switching-cost moderator.
issues.fix: Lean on the genuinely blind test instead: the pre-registered live HBM checks are the real out-of-sample and should be filed with dates and thresholds before any coding starts. Downgrade the auto-semi exercise to a consistency check and say so explicitly rather than calling it a holdout.

issues.summary: Four to six pole episodes would establish the price-versus-volume split as well as twenty to thirty, at a fraction of the cost.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The mechanism claim is a two-pole ordering: hard qualification moat holds, fungible product reprices. Polysilicon, ocean containers and MLCC (fragile pole) against aerospace forgings and LNG price-review SPAs (durable pole) span the full range and are the episodes with the richest public record including litigation. Uranium flex-down, ABF substrates, lithium offtakes and the 2017-19 memory cycle add resolution to a moderator that will already be visible, and each carries PACER, customs and multi-vendor price-series cost.
issues.what_breaks: Step 4's base rates are the first usable output and they arrive only after all 20-30 episodes are coded, so the falsifier cannot be reached early. Six data-vendor licences (TrendForce, Fastmarkets, UxC, Argus/ICIS, Drewry/Xeneta, Panjiva) are committed before anything has been shown.
issues.fix: Phase it: five pole episodes and the falsifier test first, using free sources plus one price vendor. Expand to the remaining 20 only if the two poles fail to separate cleanly, or if they separate and the moderator needs calibration for the live HBM call.

issues.summary: Making customs/bill-of-lading data the tiebreaker is unsafe for the specific live case the plan stakes itself on.
issues.why_it_applies_here: 'Where they disagree, shipment data wins' is a sensible rule for containers and polysilicon, but HBM flows move SK/TW to fabless and OSAT intermediaries largely outside US import records, and Panjiva/ImportGenius coverage of intra-Asia semiconductor shipments is thin and inconsistent over time. The pre-registered HBM checks name customs shipment tracking as one of three-to-five falsifiable tests.
issues.what_breaks: The live HBM pre-registration. A coverage gap will read as a volume decline, resolving a supplier/customer disagreement in the wrong direction and triggering a false confirmation of the fragility hypothesis in the one case that is actually blind.
issues.fix: Before pre-registering, plot HBM-relevant customs coverage by month against known shipped volumes and show the series tracks. If coverage is patchy, drop customs from the HBM check set and make the tiebreaker rule market-specific rather than global.

result.overall: As fundamental research this is unusually good — a genuine variant view (honored in volume, broken in price, split by qualification moat rather than contract label), a specific falsifier, negative controls at both poles, and honest refusal to manufacture a P&L number. But it was written for a different firm: the deliverable is a discretionary multiple haircut on one name measured over eight to twelve quarters, resting on one analyst's hand-coding of thirty contracts, none of which a replication-based committee running a days-to-weeks book can re-run or trade. Worse, the single premise that determines whether money is available — that the market actually prices disclosed LTA books as durable duration — is inherited untested and could be settled in a week with data this firm already owns; run that first, then rebuild the mechanism work as a cross-sectional EDGAR event study with the episode set as the explanatory narrative rather than the primary evidence.
